teaser: A Russian painter put himself, and the woman he loved three times over, in a doomed Roman street.
review_notes:
Opening: Edward Bulwer-Lytton saw the painting in Milan in 1833 and it is commonly cited as an inspiration for his 1834 novel The Last Days of Pompeii.
Dimensions given as about 4.5 x 6.5 m (456.5 x 651 cm).
Bryullov's visit to Pompeii dated 1827; commission by Anatoly Demidov; about six years from first sketches to completion, with the final canvas painted 1830-1833.
Identification of Countess Yuliya Samoilova as model for the mother with two daughters, the woman with a jug next to the self-portrait, and the fallen woman (traditional identification).
The group on the right as Pliny the Younger and his mother (traditional reading; Pliny was actually at Misenum, across the bay).
The pale figure in white at centre left identified as the pagan priest fleeing with temple treasures: small and faint in this image, please check the spot.
Walter Scott anecdote (sat a long time before the picture and called it an epic) is traditional.
Paris Salon 1834 gold medal; Demidov's gift to Nicholas I; line by the poet Baratynsky.
The eruption date is given as AD 79 without a month, as the traditional 24 August date is disputed.
Anecdote that Bryullov was carried out of the studio from exhaustion (traditional).
Pushkin's unfinished poem and Gogol's essay on the painting (both 1834).
Gold bracelet on the fallen woman's arm is barely visible in this image.

lesson.text: In 1834 an English novel called The Last Days of Pompeii became a bestseller. It has since been turned into operas, plays and a long line of disaster films. Its author, Edward Bulwer-Lytton, had stood in front of this canvas in Milan the year before. The modern taste for watching a city die in spectacular fashion owes a lot to one Russian painter.

Karl Bryullov was in his late twenties and living in Italy on a grant when he walked through the ruins of Pompeii in 1827. The Roman town had been buried by the volcano Vesuvius in AD 79 and was still being dug out. He stood in a street lined with tombs, just outside the city gate, and decided to paint that exact spot at the moment the sky fell.

The canvas is about 4.5 meters high and 6.5 meters wide, close to 15 by 21 feet. The figures in front are life-size. Bryullov worked on the project for about six years and, by his own account, was carried out of the studio from exhaustion more than once.

He did his homework like an archaeologist. He read the only eyewitness account, two letters by the Roman writer Pliny the Younger, who watched the eruption as a teenager. He drew vases, jewelry and street stones on site. Some poses come from the positions of bodies found under the ash. The chaos is carefully arranged in separate groups, each with its own small story.

lesson.title: Four ways to flee
lesson.text: Each cluster of people answers the same question differently: what do you save when you can save only one thing?

spots.title: The father
spots.text: A soldier in a helmet and a boy carry an old man on their arms. He raises a hand against the sky as if he could push it back. They chose to save their father.

spots.title: The cloak
spots.text: A man stretches his cloak over his wife and child like a tent. It is useless against falling rock, and it is the most natural gesture in the picture.

spots.title: Mother and son
spots.text: An old woman has sunk to the ground and will not go on. Her son bends to her, pleading. This pair is traditionally read as Pliny and his mother, taken straight from his letters.

spots.title: The bride
spots.text: A young man still wearing his wedding wreath carries his bride. Her own crown of roses is slipping off. She has fainted, or worse. He has not understood yet.

lesson.text: Notice what all four have in common. Nobody in this crowd pushes anyone aside. Nearly everybody is helping someone else. Bryullov was not interested in panic. He wanted to show people being noble at the worst moment of their lives, which is a very Romantic idea: strong feeling, raised to the level of heroism.

The bodies, though, are not Romantic at all. They are smooth, pale and perfectly proportioned, like Greek marble statues that happen to be running. That mix is what made the picture a sensation: the polished drawing of the old academies, lit by fire and fear.

One face returns again and again. Countess Yuliya Samoilova, a wealthy and famously independent Russian aristocrat, was Bryullov's close companion for years. She is thought to be the model for at least three women in the crowd.

And the painter did not stop at including her. He wrote himself into the disaster as well, as a man saving the tools of his trade. He is in the left half, among the people pouring down the steps of a tomb.
Bryullov is here, looking up at the sky with his paint box balanced on his head. Where?

spots.title: The painter
spots.text: A fair-haired young man with a box of brushes and paints on his head: an artist of ancient Pompeii with Bryullov's face. Beside him, a woman with a jug is one of the Samoilova look-alikes.

lesson.text: He is the only person here who is looking rather than fleeing. It is a claim as much as a signature: the artist is the witness. Now follow his eyes upward, because the sky explains why this painting looks so strange and so theatrical.
Two lights fight over the street, and they have different colors.

lines.label: Lightning, cold and white
lines.text: A flash from the upper right throws a hard white light onto the people in front. It is why their skin looks like marble and their shadows are so sharp.

lines.label: The volcano, hot and red
lines.text: Behind them, Vesuvius colors the smoke and the back of the street red. It lights only the distance. The foreground belongs to the lightning.

lines.label: A parted crowd
lines.text: The groups form two wings that open in the middle, like a stage curtain. In the gap, alone on the paving stones, lies the figure the lightning hits hardest.

lesson.text: That figure is a woman in yellow who has fallen from a chariot. You can see it racing away behind her, its axle broken, the horses out of control. Her jewels are scattered on the stones. Her baby, alive, reaches for her. Bryullov places this mother and child at the dead center of the bottom edge, where no viewer can avoid them.
Bryullov treats a natural disaster as a moral drama: the old world dies in the center of the picture, and around it people show who they are by what they try to save.

The painting toured like a rock star. It drew crowds in Rome and Milan, won a gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1834, then sailed to Saint Petersburg. The novelist Walter Scott is said to have sat in front of it for a long time and called it not a painting but an epic.

In Russia the reaction was closer to delirium. No Russian painter had ever been cheered across Europe before. The poet Pushkin began a poem about it, Gogol wrote an essay, and a line of verse went around: the last day of Pompeii had become the first day of the Russian brush.

lesson.title: The edges of the stage
lesson.text: The famous groups hold the middle. The corners carry the larger meaning.

spots.title: Falling gods
spots.text: Statues topple from a rooftop, caught in mid-air by the lightning. They are the gods of Rome. The city's religion is collapsing along with its walls.

spots.title: The Christian priest
spots.text: At the far left a bearded man in a red hood holds a torch and a hanging incense burner. He looks up calmly at the sky. For Bryullov he stands for the new faith that will outlive this world.

spots.title: The rearing horse
spots.text: A white horse rears in terror and its rider can barely stay on. Animals, in this picture, are the only ones allowed pure panic.

lesson.text: The man who paid for all this, the industrial heir Anatoly Demidov, gave the canvas to Tsar Nicholas I. It hung at the Academy of Arts as a model for students, and since 1897 it has belonged to the Russian Museum. Bryullov, nicknamed “Karl the Great” at home, never produced anything as big or as successful again.

spots.title: Mother and daughters
spots.text: A kneeling mother gathers her two girls in her arms and stares upward. Her features are those of Countess Samoilova.

spots.title: The fallen woman
spots.text: Lying on her back in a yellow dress, hair spread on the stones. Her baby leans on her chest. Around her arm, a gold bracelet of the kind found in the excavations.

spots.title: The pagan priest
spots.text: A pale figure in white hurries away clutching shining objects: the temple's treasures. Compare him with the calm Christian priest on the left. Bryullov is taking sides.

spots.title: The runaway chariot
spots.text: Half lost in the glare, a chariot bolts toward the back of the street with its driver thrown off balance. It is the vehicle the woman in yellow fell from.

spots.title: The tombs
spots.text: These pitted stone monuments are real. They still line the Street of Tombs at Pompeii. Bryullov has them cracking and leaning over the crowd.

spots.title: A face in the middle
spots.text: A woman in a pale headscarf bites her fingers and stares out to the side. Fear here has no grand gesture, only wide eyes.

spots.title: Fire in the sky
spots.text: The red is laid over the black smoke in streaks, with sparks of yellow. Vesuvius itself is off to the right, mostly hidden: you see what it does, not the mountain.

lesson.text: Today the picture can look overacted, like a silent film frozen at its loudest frame. That is fair, and it is also the point of the comparison. Long before cinema existed, Bryullov worked out how a disaster movie holds an audience: a huge spectacle behind, and in front of it a few faces you are made to care about.

quiz.question: Which ancient text did Bryullov use as his eyewitness source?
options: The letters of Pliny the Younger
The diary of a Roman emperor
quiz.explanation: Pliny the Younger watched the eruption as a teenager and described it in two letters.

quiz.question: How does Bryullov show himself in the painting?
options: As a soldier carrying his father
As a priest with a torch
As an artist with a paint box on his head
quiz.explanation: He appears on the left as a fair-haired painter saving his box of brushes and paints.

quiz.question: What lights the figures in the foreground?
options: A cold white flash of lightning
The red glow of the volcano
quiz.explanation: The lightning lights the front of the scene, while the volcano's red glow lights only the background.

quiz.question: What do the statues falling from the roof stand for?
options: The collapse of the old Roman religion
quiz.explanation: They are the gods of Rome, falling together with the city.

quiz.question: What happened to the woman in yellow at the center?
quiz.explanation: She fell from the chariot that is racing away behind her with a broken axle.

quiz.question: Who is thought to be the model for several women in the crowd?
quiz.explanation: Samoilova, the painter's close companion, appears at least three times.

facts.text: The street in the painting is a real place in Pompeii that Bryullov visited.
facts.explanation: It is the Street of Tombs outside the city gate, which he drew on site in 1827.

facts.text: Most people in the painting are shoving others out of their way to escape.
facts.explanation: Almost everyone is helping somebody else, which was Bryullov's way of making them heroic.

facts.text: The painting was first shown in Saint Petersburg and only later traveled to Italy.
facts.explanation: It was shown in Rome, Milan and Paris before it reached Russia.
